Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Liver lesions are limited to two lesions (segments VII and VIII) with a maximum diameter of 5.2 cm, suggesting a technically feasible hepatic resection (right hepatectomy or extended right hepatectomy).  
- However, critical information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing:  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatibility with surgery (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery – Missing).  
  • Presence of vascular contact or invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion – Missing) and detailed arterial anatomy (ArterialAnatomy – Missing).  
  • Status of the primary colorectal tumor (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected? – Missing) and any obstructive or bleeding symptoms (Missing).  
- Because these missing data directly impact whether a safe, curative resection can be performed, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending clarification of these points.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic therapy adjustment – Switch to a second‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) given progression on FOLFOX and KRAS‑mutated status (no anti‑EGFR benefit).  
2. Restaging after 2–3 cycles – Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to:  
   • Define lesion borders, vascular involvement, and biliary anatomy.  
   • Re‑assess FLR volume (CT volumetry or MRI).  
3. Evaluation of the primary tumor – Perform colonoscopy and cross‑sectional imaging of the right colon to determine resectability, presence of obstruction, perforation, or bleeding. If resectable and symptomatic, plan right hemicolectomy.  
4. Multidisciplinary decision –  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in a cirrhotic liver) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to curative surgery.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the future remnant, then re‑image to confirm adequacy.  
5. Surgical sequencing –  
   • Preferred simultaneous resection (right hemicolectomy + right hepatectomy) in a fit 71‑year‑old if operative risk acceptable and FLR adequate.  
   • If operative risk high or FLR marginal, adopt a staged approach: first resect the colon primary, allow recovery, then perform liver resection (or PVE‑induced hypertrophy) after systemic disease control.  
6. Post‑operative systemic therapy – Resume or continue second‑line chemotherapy (FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) for at least 3–6 months post‑resection, with serial CEA monitoring (baseline 950 ng/mL) and imaging every 3 months.  
7. Clinical trial consideration – Evaluate eligibility for trials targeting KRAS‑mutated metastatic colorectal cancer (e.g., KRAS‑G12C inhibitors, immunotherapy combinations) given aggressive disease biology.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- FLR ratio compatibility with surgery (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio).  
- Presence and extent of vascular contact/invasion and detailed arterial anatomy (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, ArterialAnatomy).  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or not) and any obstructive/bleeding symptoms (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization, PresenceOfSymptomsForObstruction/Perforation/Bleeding).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (GradeOfDifferentation).  
- Results of liver MRI (Has liver MRI been performed?).  
- Assessment for brain metastasis (ExtrahepaticBrainInvolvement).  

These items are essential to finalize resectability judgment and to design a safe, curative surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all liver lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
F. Previous systemic treatments received and tolerance.
G. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears.
H. Evolution of CEA after first-line chemotherapy.
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
1. Completeness:
- Recommendation 1 categorizes the liver metastases as potentially resectable pending further details, while Recommendation 2 deems them unresectable due to progression under FOLFOX, highlighting divergent comprehensiveness in their approach to surgical candidacy and management.
- Recommendation 1 provides a detailed surgical and postoperative plan contingent on further assessment, whereas Recommendation 2 focuses mainly on systemic therapy and reassessment but lacks a detailed surgical plan.
- Recommendation 1 also includes specific strategies for postoperative care and clinical trial considerations that Recommendation 2 does not cover.

2. Step-by-step concordance:
- Step 1: The assessment of resectability differs significantly; Recommendation 1 considers the lesions potentially resectable pending further data, while Recommendation 2 determines them as currently unresectable due to aggressive disease progression.
- Step 2: The proposed management strategies differ; Recommendation 1 outlines a clear pathway including surgical intervention upon meeting certain criteria, whereas Recommendation 2 dismisses immediate surgical options and focuses on systemic therapy adaptation.

3. Case-tailoring concordance:
- Recommendation 1 includes specific case-tailored considerations such as the suitability of simultaneous versus staged surgical interventions based on patient’s operative risk, which Recommendation 2 does not discuss.
- Recommendation 1 also considers potential eligibility for clinical trials targeting KRAS mutations and the implications of the patient's fitness level, which is absent in Recommendation 2.

4. Missing data concordance:
- Both recommendations identify missing data, but there are significant differences. For instance, Recommendation 1 emphasizes FLR ratio and vascular anatomy, while Recommendation 2 emphasizes the need for a detailed assessment of the liver lesions and extrahepatic disease status. This reflects a lack of concordance in identifying critical missing information.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The MDT already judged that the current disease burden does not meet criteria for immediate resection. Critical information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing, specifically:  
- Complete cross‑sectional staging (contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT and liver MRI) to define the exact hepatic segmental distribution, vascular or biliary involvement, and to rule out extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional adequacy.  
- Confirmation of whether the primary right‑colon tumor has already been resected or remains in situ.  
Because these decisive data are absent, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront”; however, there is no absolute contraindication (e.g., unresectable extra‑hepatic disease or inadequate FLR) that would place it in “Not resectable.” Hence, the lesion set is considered potentially resectable pending further work‑up and/or additional down‑staging therapy.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging work‑up  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis.  
   - Perform liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to delineate lesion number, segmental location, relationship to portal/hepatic veins and biliary ducts.  
   - If any extra‑hepatic sites are identified, document extent.  

2. Molecular profiling of the primary tumor (if tissue available)  
   - Test for KRAS, NRAS, BRAF mutations and microsatellite instability/mismatch repair status. Results will guide choice of targeted agents (e.g., anti‑EGFR vs. anti‑VEGF) and eligibility for immunotherapy.  

3. Evaluate need for primary‑tumor control  
   - If the right‑colon primary has not been resected and is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or at high risk of complications, schedule a right hemicolectomy either before or concurrently with liver surgery (staged approach).  

4. Systemic therapy optimisation  
   - Continue or modify chemotherapy based on response and molecular profile (e.g., FOLFOX/FOLFIRI plus appropriate biologic).  
   - Consider conversion therapy with intensified regimen or addition of targeted agents to achieve further tumor shrinkage, aiming for lesions ≤5 cm and clear vascular margins.  

5. Re‑assessment after additional systemic therapy (typically after 2–3 more cycles)  
   - Repeat liver MRI and CT chest/abdomen to evaluate tumor response, FLR, and any new extra‑hepatic disease.  

6. Surgical planning (if re‑assessment shows resectable disease)  
   - Plan an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy that removes all three lesions with negative margins while preserving ≥30 % FLR in a non‑cirrhotic liver (or ≥40 % if underlying liver disease).  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization or two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   - Coordinate simultaneous or staged resection of the primary colon tumor based on its status and patient fitness.  

7. Post‑operative adjuvant strategy  
   - Resume systemic therapy post‑resection (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± biologic) and consider enrollment in clinical trials if appropriate.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for decision‑making)  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. intact, symptomatic vs. asymptomatic).  
- Molecular phenotype of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS/BRAF/MSI status).  
- Detailed hepatic anatomy: specific segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, arterial anatomy.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and functional assessment.  
- Complete staging imaging results (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, liver MRI) to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, brain).  

These items must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the residual lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for further systemic therapy.
D. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.
E. Previous systemic regimens received and tolerance.
F. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case a surgical window appears.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations differ significantly in several areas:

1. **Completeness:**
   - **Recommendation 1** classifies the liver metastases as 'potentially resectable,' pending further staging and systemic treatment efforts, and outlines an extensive plan for surgical and systemic management, including imaging, molecular profiling, and surgery.
   - **Recommendation 2** deems the metastases 'unresectable' at present due to bulky lesions and limited chemotherapy response, focusing on adapting systemic therapy, close radiological monitoring, and potential conversion to a resectable state only if significant tumor downsizing is achieved.
   - The differences in resectability assessment and subsequent management plans reflect a lack of completeness alignment, as one plan focuses on further staging and potential resection, while the other prioritizes systemic therapy adaptation due to current unresectability.
   
2. **Step-by-step concordance:**
   - The first recommendation follows a stepwise approach of staging, systemic therapy, reassessment, and surgical planning if resectability is achieved.
   - The second recommendation immediately considers the situation as unresectable and emphasizes systemic therapy modification and monitoring, with resection reconsideration only upon substantial response.
   - These divergent approaches illustrate a lack of step concordance, as they do not share the same initial resectability assessment or management sequence.

3. **Case-tailoring concordance:**
   - **Recommendation 1** provides detailed case-specific plans, including potential surgical interventions and criteria based on liver remnant volume and primary tumor status.
   - **Recommendation 2** focuses more generally on systemic therapy adaptation and monitoring without specifying similar surgical or molecular profiling details that might tailor the approach further to the case specifics.
   - The lack of detailed case tailoring in Recommendation 2 compared to the comprehensive individualized plan in Recommendation 1 indicates a lack of case-tailoring alignment.
   
4. **Missing data concordance:**
   - Both recommendations identify missing clinical information, but there is no complete overlap in the specifics they highlight.
   - **Recommendation 1** emphasizes detailed imaging, molecular phenotype, and primary tumor status, while **Recommendation 2** includes patient performance status and new elements like liquid biopsies, without focusing as much on the molecular profiling or imaging detail specified in Recommendation 1.
   - The differences in identified missing information suggest a lack of missing data concordance.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left hepatectomy performed two years prior. Liver MRI: three new lesions (segments V, VI, VII) measuring 1.5 to 2.8 cm.On the thoracic CT scan no other metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 480 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Multiple liver recurrence, feasibility of local treatment to be re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has three metachronous liver metastases (segments V‑VI‑VII) after a prior left hepatectomy, leaving only right‑lobe parenchyma. Whether a curative resection can be performed depends on (a) the future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio after removal of the involved segments, which is currently missing, and (b) the presence or absence of vascular (portal/hepatic artery) involvement, also not reported. These two pieces of information are decisive for surgical feasibility; therefore resection cannot be declared upfront and is not excluded outright. A staged approach (e.g., portal vein embolization or two‑stage hepatectomy) may be required once the missing data are clarified.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFOXIRI combined with anti‑VEGF therapy) because the disease is multiple, KRAS‑mutated, and CEA is markedly elevated, indicating biologically aggressive disease.  
- Obtain a high‑quality contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver with volumetric analysis to calculate the FLR ratio and to delineate hepatic arterial and portal venous anatomy, as well as any vascular contact of the lesions.  
- If FLR is insufficient (<30 % in a normal liver, <40 % after prior major resection) and no major vascular invasion is seen, proceed with portal vein embolization of the right portal branches that will be resected to hypertrophy the remaining left‑over segments (segments I‑VIII‑IVa) before definitive surgery.  
- Re‑image 4–6 weeks after PVE; if FLR has increased to an acceptable level and lesions remain resectable, perform an anatomic right‑trisectionectomy or limited segmental resections (segments V‑VI‑VII) with negative margins, preserving segment VIII and caudate (segment I).  
- If vascular invasion is present or FLR cannot be achieved despite PVE, consider alternative local therapies (e.g., percutaneous radiofrequency or microwave ablation) combined with continued systemic treatment.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA and repeat thoraco‑abdominal imaging to ensure no new extra‑hepatic disease emerges.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative FLR ratio (volumetric assessment) – essential to decide if immediate resection, PVE, or staged approach is possible.  
- Detailed vascular involvement (portal/hepatic artery contact or invasion) – determines resectability and need for vascular reconstruction.  
- Arterial anatomy (variant hepatic arterial supply) – influences surgical planning and safety of resection.  
- Status of systemic therapy already given (yes/no, regimen, response) – impacts timing of surgery.  
- Confirmation of primary colorectal tumor resection and its location/grade – influences overall oncologic strategy and need for additional colorectal surgery.  
- Presence of extra‑hepatic lymph‑node metastasis or brain metastasis – would upstage disease and potentially preclude curative liver surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three metachronous liver metastases (segments V, VI, VII; 1.5–2.8 cm) occurring after a prior left hepatectomy, without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesions are located in the only remaining right liver and appear peripherally distributed. Resection may be technically feasible with a strict parenchymal-sparing strategy while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of previous major hepatectomy, this pattern is considered potentially resectable, pending detailed vascular and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and volumetric assessment
• Perform expert liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to precisely define vascular and biliary relationships of the three lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (which is the current liver) and assess portal inflow and hepatic venous outflow.
• Given the high CEA level (480 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA level (480 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows assessment of tumor biology and potential further downsizing.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing mandatory)
• If resectability is confirmed, proceed with ultrasound-guided wedge/segmental resections or ablation of segments V, VI, and VII.
• Avoid any major resection and preserve maximal functional parenchyma.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three lesions on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Patient’s current liver function and performance status.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the left hepatectomy.
E. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular profile of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
F. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
Completeness: Both recommendations cover the necessary domains such as resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. They both address the need for volumetric assessment and detailed vascular analysis, systemic chemotherapy, and follow-up protocols, making them aligned in this aspect.

Step-by-step concordance: Both recommendations identify the case as potentially resectable and suggest a similar sequence of actions involving preoperative imaging, systemic chemotherapy, followed by surgical resection, making them concordant in terms of steps.

Case-tailoring concordance: Recommendation 1 discusses the KRAS mutation's impact on therapy, but Recommendation 2 excludes anti-EGFR therapy due to the KRAS mutation, which is somewhat aligned but not fully. Recommendation 2 introduces patient-specific surgical considerations like minimally invasive approaches and prehabilitation protocols, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. 

Missing data concordance: While both mention the need for volumetric and vascular assessments, Recommendation 2 includes criteria like liver function, performance status, and molecular profile of the primary cancer, which Recommendation 1 does not list explicitly, resulting in a lack of alignment in missing data identification.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, history of segment VII resection. Liver MRI: local recurrence at resection site (2.5 cm) and additional nodule segment V. No other lesion at the thoraco CT scan CEA 410 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Localized recurrence on resection scar, complex technical feasibility.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has two liver metastases (segment VII recurrence 2.5 cm and a new nodule in segment V) with no extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑CT. However, critical information that directly determines surgical feasibility is missing: future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, extent of vascular contact/invasion, arterial anatomy, and baseline liver function. Without these data we cannot confirm that a safe, curative resection can be performed now; therefore the case is classified as potentially resectable pending further evaluation and/or pre‑operative optimization.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Obtain missing pre‑operative data:  
  – Perform contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry (or MRI) to calculate FLR ratio and assess liver parenchyma quality.  
  – Review contrast‑enhanced imaging (or repeat MRI/CT) to define vascular relationships of both lesions (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery).  
  – Obtain liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance if available) and assess performance status.  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) as neoadjuvant treatment to:  
  – Evaluate tumor biology (response of CEA, radiologic shrinkage).  
  – Potentially downsize lesions if vascular involvement is borderline.  
• Re‑image after 2–3 cycles of chemotherapy: repeat MRI and CT volumetry.  
  – If FLR is <30 % (or <40 % in a steatotic liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left lobe before resection.  
• Once adequate FLR and clear vascular anatomy are confirmed, proceed to repeat hepatic resection:  
  – Parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of the recurrent lesion in segment VII and segmentectomy or wedge resection of the segment V nodule, using intra‑operative ultrasound to achieve R0 margins.  
  – Ensure preservation of sufficient functional liver tissue.  
• Post‑operative management:  
  – Resume/adapt systemic therapy based on pathological response and molecular profile (once obtained).  
  – Monitor CEA serially; consider adjuvant chemotherapy if high‑risk features are present.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
The most crucial missing items that must be obtained to finalize the plan are:  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatibility with surgery.  
• Presence and extent of vascular contact or invasion (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery).  
• Detailed arterial anatomy and any variant anatomy.  
• Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
• Status of prior systemic therapy (has chemotherapy already been given?).  
• Molecular phenotype and grade of the primary colorectal tumor (to guide systemic regimen).
Reference:

The patient presents with a 2.5 cm local recurrence at the prior segment VII resection site and an additional nodule in segment V, without reported extrahepatic disease. This represents localized intrahepatic recurrence in a previously operated posterior segment. Despite the scar location and technical complexity, both lesions appear amenable to local treatment while preserving adequate inflow/outflow and functional reserve. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria in the setting of prior liver resection, this pattern is considered potentially resectable, pending detailed vascular and volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and anatomical assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define the relationship of the segment VII recurrence to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and scar tissue.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (current liver) and assess inflow/outflow preservation.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Consider peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the elevated CEA (410 ng/mL) and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

B. Combined local treatment strategy
• Given the scar location and technical difficulty, a combined approach is appropriate:
– Either Parenchymal-sparing resection or thermo-ablation of the segment V lesion.
– Resection of the segment VII scar recurrence depending on its relationship to vascular structures and the extent of adhesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both approaches.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles if administered.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment VII recurrence on MRI.
B. Exact volumetric assessment of the remaining liver (future liver remnant).
C. Patient’s current liver function and performance status.
D. Details of previous chemotherapy received before/after the prior liver surgery.
E. Confirmation of absence of extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
G. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Details of timing between previous resection and current recurrence
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
**Completeness:** Both recommendations cover critical areas: resectability assessment, preoperative imaging/staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy. Recommendation 1 emphasizes preoperative chemotherapy and assesses FLR after chemotherapy, whereas Recommendation 2 suggests detailed preoperative imaging/staging before deciding on potential peri-operative chemotherapy. Despite this subtle difference, both recommendations broadly address the same components necessary for a comprehensive management plan. Therefore, they align in completeness.

**Step-by-step concordance:** In Step 1, both classify the case as potentially resectable pending further evaluation. In Step 2, both recommendations outline a structured approach to obtain missing data, consider peri-operative systemic therapy, and aim for R0 resection with emphasis on minimally invasive techniques. The management plan sequences are similar, hence they align in step-by-step reasoning.

They differ in the level of detail regarding patient-specific factors and tailored surgical approaches (e.g., minimally invasive methods). Hence, they are not aligned in case-tailoring.

Although Recommendation 2 includes additional details like liquid biopsy, the essential missing data remain consistent across both. Therefore, they align in missing data concordance.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, history of segmental VI-VII resection. Liver MRI: new lesion segment III (2.4 cm) and micronodule segment II. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous contralateral recurrence, possible minimally invasive approach depending on remnant volume.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the two left‑lateral lesions (segments II and III) are technically amenable to resection, but decisive information is missing. A thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) is required to exclude extra‑hepatic disease, and an accurate future liver remnant (FLR) ratio calculation is needed to confirm that the remaining liver after a left lateral sectionectomy (in the setting of a prior segmental VI‑VII resection) will be sufficient. Until these data are obtained, surgery cannot be planned safely.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Obtain comprehensive staging: contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and repeat liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to evaluate vascular contact, biliary involvement, and to calculate FLR volume.  
- Measure serum CEA and document status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected or pending).  
- If staging confirms absence of extra‑hepatic disease and FLR ≥30 % (≥20 % in patients with chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery: minimally invasive left lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) with parenchymal‑sparing technique, preserving segment IV and the previously resected right posterior sector. Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate the micronodule in segment II and to assess margins.  
- If FLR is borderline, consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left medial sector (segment IV) before resection.  
- In parallel, initiate peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3‑4 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) given the metachronous nature of the disease and to treat any occult micrometastases. Adjust the sequence based on FLR assessment: neoadjuvant chemotherapy first if FLR is adequate, or PVE followed by chemotherapy if hypertrophy is needed.  
- Post‑operative follow‑up with serial CEA and imaging at 3‑month intervals; consider adjuvant chemotherapy if pathology shows high‑risk features (poor differentiation, vascular invasion, etc.).

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone, or brain metastases.  
- Quantitative FLR ratio and detailed volumetric analysis of the remnant liver.  
- Detailed vascular anatomy and any tumor‑vessel contact in segments II‑III.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs. pending) and current CEA level.  
- History of systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles, response). These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two metachronous liver lesions after prior segment VI–VII resection: a 2.4 cm metastasis in segment III and a micronodule in segment II, without reported extrahepatic disease. Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, mid-rectal T3N1 tumor with five bilobar liver metastases and a right lung metastasis at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 330 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, evaluation of a possible combined approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The case cannot be declared resectable upfront because decisive information is lacking. Specifically, the size, segmental distribution and vascular/biliary involvement of the five bilobar liver lesions, the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and the resectability of the right‑lung metastasis are not provided. Moreover, the primary rectal tumor has not yet been addressed (resection status, need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy). These missing data require neoadjuvant systemic therapy and further imaging before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for RAS‑wild‑type, synchronous metastatic disease (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or FOLFOX + cetuximab).  
• After 2–3 months, restage with high‑resolution liver MRI, PET‑CT, and repeat chest CT to:  
    – Determine response of liver lesions, exact size, segmental involvement, and any vascular/biliary contact.  
    – Calculate FLR ratio and decide if portal vein embolization or staged hepatectomy is needed.  
    – Assess the right‑lung nodule for size, location relative to vessels/bronchi and resectability.  
• If imaging shows that all liver lesions can be cleared with an adequate FLR (≥20 % in a normal liver, ≥30 % after chemotherapy), plan a combined or staged surgical approach:  
    – Primary rectal cancer: proceed with total mesorectal excision; if the tumor remains T3 with threatened margin, give neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy before resection.  
    – Liver: perform parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy of all five lesions; if FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization first or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS.  
    – Lung: if the solitary right‑lung metastasis is technically resectable, schedule pulmonary metastasectomy (segmentectomy or wedge) either synchronously with liver surgery (if patient fitness permits) or in a staged fashion after hepatic resection. If not surgically resectable, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant therapy: continue systemic treatment (e.g., maintenance bevacizumab or anti‑EGFR) and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Exact size, segmental location and vascular/biliary involvement of each liver metastasis.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and ratio to total liver.  
- Resectability assessment of the right‑lung metastasis (size, lobar distribution, relation to bronchi/vessels).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (has it been resected? need for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy?).  
- Histologic grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.  
- Confirmation of systemic therapy already given (if any) and response assessment.  
- PET‑CT results to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

These pieces of information are required to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases and a single right lung metastasis in the setting of a mid-rectal T3N1 tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not contraindicate a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease may be amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections provided adequate future liver remnant is preserved. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (330 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Resectability assessment of the lung lesion by thoracic surgery.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
H. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
The two recommendations are substantially similar as they both cover the major clinical domains and management components required for treating a patient with a primary colorectal tumor and liver metastases, with possible extrahepatic metastases (lung). 

1. **Completeness**: Both recommendations address resectability assessment, preoperative staging (via imaging), systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative therapy and surveillance. They emphasize the importance of systemic therapy given the RAS wild-type status, detailed imaging to assess resectability, and potential surgical approaches including parenchymal-sparing hepatectomy, and management of the rectal primary and lung metastasis. 

2. **Step-by-Step Concordance**: In Step 1, both recommendations consider the patient potentially resectable, requiring additional information before making a definitive surgical plan. In Step 2, both suggest initial systemic therapy, followed by detailed imaging and reassessment, and potential resection if sufficient tumor response is achieved. The sequence of imaging, systemic therapy, and evaluation aligns closely.

3. **Case-Tailoring Concordance**: Both recommendations take into account case-specific factors such as the molecular profile (RAS wild-type), potential need for portal vein embolization, and specific surgical tactics like parenchymal-sparing approaches or ALPPS. Both also integrate considerations for the patient's overall treatment tolerance and potential for surgical recovery.

4. **Missing Data Concordance**: Both recommendations highlight the need for precise information on the liver metastases' segmental distribution, resectability of the lung metastasis, future liver remnant estimation, status of the primary rectal tumor, and the absence of other extrahepatic disease. They also consider the patient's molecular profile, performance status, and tumor biology markers.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has seven liver metastases (2‑5 cm) but critical information required to determine immediate surgical feasibility is missing: hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and whether the primary colon tumor has already been resected. Because these data are decisive for planning a curative hepatectomy, surgery cannot be performed upfront; it will require down‑staging systemic therapy and further imaging to clarify anatomic resectability.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive systemic therapy appropriate for BRAF‑mutated, MSS colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab, or a BRAF‑targeted regimen such as encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib per BEACON).  
- Simultaneously evaluate the primary tumor: if symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or if it remains unresected, schedule colon resection either before or after the first cycles of chemotherapy, depending on clinical urgency.  
- Obtain a dedicated liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast to define the exact segmental distribution of all lesions, assess vascular/biliary involvement, and calculate the FLR volume.  
- After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, restage with repeat imaging (CT + MRI). If tumor burden has decreased and a clear anatomical plan emerges, calculate the FLR ratio; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % in a compromised liver), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to augment FLR.  
- If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows that all lesions can be cleared with an adequate FLR and without compromising major vascular structures, proceed to curative liver resection (single‑stage if feasible, otherwise a two‑stage or ALPPS approach).  
- If adequate down‑staging is not achieved or anatomic constraints persist, continue systemic therapy and discuss enrollment in clinical trials or best‑supportive care, given the poor prognostic impact of BRAF V600E.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Status of primary tumor resection (has it been removed?).  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement and presence/extent of vascular or biliary invasion.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio compatible with safe hepatectomy.  
- Results of liver MRI (lesion mapping, volumetry).  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and any prior systemic therapy.  
- Confirmation of absence of brain metastases (imaging not reported).  

These items are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven liver metastases (2–5 cm) in the setting of a right T4aN2 colon cancer and a BRAF V600E mutation with very high CEA (1600 ng/mL). Despite the disease being confined to the liver, the number of lesions, their size, and especially the unfavorable molecular profile indicate highly aggressive systemic tumor biology. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 7 lesions to vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.
• Given the high CEA level (1600 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• The elevated CEA level (1600 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Initiate intensive systemic therapy adapted to the BRAF V600E profile according to MDT decision : give 3-6 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS status is unknow but BRAF V600E profile is poor prognostic factor
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with marked reduction in number and size of lesions. 
• In this situation, first multiple atypical resections and ablation guided by ultrasound with the aim to obtain R0 margins.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective.

E. If disease remains extensive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the 7 lesions and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
E. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
Reasoning:
**Completeness:** Both recommendations cover the same major components: assessment of resectability, preoperative staging with imaging, the use of systemic therapy, surgical management considerations, and postoperative strategy. They recognize the need for systemic therapy due to the unfavorable BRAF mutation and potential resectability after downstaging. Thus, they are aligned in completeness.

**Step-by-step concordance:** The recommendations agree on the initial assessment of 'potentially resectable' given the liver metastases and aggressive tumor biology, followed by the necessity of systemic therapy. They also propose similar steps for imaging and reassessing resectability after chemotherapy. Therefore, they show step concordance.

**Case-tailoring concordance:** There are differences in the considerations for the sequence and type of systemic therapy, with Recommendation 1 specifically tailoring therapy to BRAF-mutated MSS disease. Recommendation 2 discusses KRAS status and potential liquid biopsy, which Recommendation 1 does not mention. These differences in molecular profiling and specific systemic therapy considerations show a lack of case-tailoring concordance.

**Missing data concordance:** There is a partial overlap in the missing information identified (detailed hepatic anatomy and vascular/biliary relationships), but Recommendation 1 focuses on the surgical aspect like FLR and absence of brain metastases, whereas Recommendation 2 emphasizes tumor biology aspects like differentiation grade, nutritional status, and circulating tumor markers, which are not mentioned in Recommendation 1. Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- The liver MRI shows a segment VII metastasis with >1 cm IVC invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion: True). Such major vascular involvement generally precludes immediate resection without further planning or down‑staging.  
- Critical information required to decide feasibility is missing: thoraco‑abdominal CT for extra‑hepatic disease (ThoracoCTScanPerformed: False), future liver remnant adequacy (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery: Missing), and the status of the primary colon lesion (Has the colorectal primary tumor been already resected?: Missing).  
- Because these missing data are decisive for operative planning (need to confirm no extra‑hepatic disease and sufficient FLR, and to decide on simultaneous vs staged colon resection), the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending those prerequisites.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging: obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary, peritoneal, nodal, bone or brain metastases.  
2. Assess liver functional reserve: calculate FLR volume on CT volumetry; if FLR <30 % (or <40 % after chemotherapy), plan portal vein embolization or ALPPS to augment FLR.  
3. Initiate systemic therapy: start a 2–3 month regimen of doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with a biologic agent appropriate for RAS‑wild type disease (e.g., anti‑EGFR such as cetuximab) to (a) treat occult extra‑hepatic disease, (b) assess tumor biology, and (c) attempt to downsize the IVC‑invading lesion.  
4. Re‑image after systemic therapy (MRI liver + CT chest/abdomen): evaluate response of the IVC‑involved metastasis and overall disease burden.  
5. If disease remains limited to the liver, FLR is adequate, and no extra‑hepatic lesions are identified:  
   a. Plan definitive surgery.  
   b. If the primary colon tumor has not yet been resected, perform a staged or simultaneous colectomy (preferably staged if extensive liver surgery is anticipated).  
   c. Proceed with liver resection of all four metastases, employing total hepatic vascular exclusion and IVC resection with graft reconstruction (vascular surgery collaboration).  
   d. Ensure intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins and to detect additional lesions.  
6. If after systemic therapy the IVC involvement persists with no safe reconstructive option, or extra‑hepatic disease emerges, shift to a palliative systemic approach or consider locoregional therapies (e.g., Y‑90 radioembolisation) as appropriate.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoraco‑abdominal imaging results (presence/absence of extra‑hepatic metastases).  
- Future liver remnant volume and functional assessment (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery).  
- Status of the primary colon tumor (resected vs pending).  
- Exact size of each hepatic lesion (Maximum/MinimumLesionDiameter) and arterial/portal anatomy to plan resection and reconstruction.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered (LiverMetastasesUnderSystemicTreatment).  

These items are essential to finalize resectability and to design the definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. While the number of lesions is limited, true caval invasion makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unlikely without complex vascular resection/reconstruction and carries high operative risk. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships and a chest CT scan.
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with or without partial IVC resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with vascular surgery is required to assess feasibility of partial IVC resection/reconstruction if needed.

C. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• One or two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• If regression of caval invasion occurs or reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of all lesions.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or graft reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships on liver MRI : precise extent and depth of IVC invasion
B. Baseline future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of two-stage strategy with major hepatectomy.
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for intensive chemotherapy and for potential major liver surgery including complex vascular surgery.
E. Presence or absence of any extrahepatic disease on full staging.
F. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
I. a chest CT scan
Reasoning:
1. **Completeness**: Both recommendations address the major clinical domains required for managing colorectal cancer with liver metastases, including resectability assessment, preoperative staging, systemic therapy, surgical management, and postoperative plans. They both suggest advanced imaging, systemic chemotherapy, and detailed surgical planning involving complex liver and potential IVC resection. Thus, they cover the same essential clinical management areas.

2. **Step-by-step Concordance**: Both recommendations follow a similar logical progression: assessing resectability based on liver metastases and IVC invasion, recommending systemic chemotherapy tailored to tumor biology, and planning surgical intervention contingent on response and feasibility. The sequencing and clinical reasoning align closely, with both advocating for a multidisciplinary approach.

3. **Case-tailoring Concordance**: Both recommendations are tailored to the specifics of the case, considering factors like RAS-wild type status for chemotherapy selection, the high CEA level, and potential need for complex vascular procedures. They both emphasize the need for detailed imaging and specific therapeutic strategies aligned with the patient's unique clinical presentation.

4. **Missing Data Concordance**: While there are overlaps in the missing data identified (e.g., need for comprehensive imaging to rule out extrahepatic disease), Recommendation 2 delves deeper into additional aspects like ctDNA, CTCs, and the primary tumor's grade of differentiation, which are not addressed in Recommendation 1. Thus, there is a lack of complete alignment on the missing clinical information that needs to be acquired.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, five liver metastases including one 8.5 cm in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 870 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis with bilateral portal contact, complex technical discussion.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver disease includes a large (8.5 cm) central metastasis in segment IVb with bilateral portal contact, making a one‑stage anatomic resection technically demanding and dependent on the future liver remnant (FLR) volume and arterial anatomy, both of which are missing. In addition, the primary right‑colon tumor has not been documented as resected, and no systemic therapy has been reported. Therefore, definitive resection cannot be performed upfront; it will require (a) control of the primary tumor, (b) neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy (with possible down‑staging), and (c) definitive FLR assessment (volumetry, possible portal vein embolization) before a curative liver operation can be planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Confirm and stage the primary colon cancer: obtain colonoscopy report, assess for obstruction, perforation or bleeding; if not yet resected, schedule primary tumor resection (or simultaneous resection if feasible after down‑staging).  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated, right‑sided colon cancer (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) aiming for tumor and liver metastasis downsizing.  
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, restage with high‑resolution liver MRI (including diffusion‑weighted imaging and hepatobiliary contrast) to define lesion number, vascular involvement, and to evaluate arterial anatomy.  
• Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR ratio; if FLR is insufficient (<30 % in a normal liver, <40 % after chemotherapy), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a staged approach (e.g., ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
• Re‑assess resectability after down‑staging and FLR augmentation: plan a curative liver resection (potentially extended left hepatectomy or right trisectionectomy with segment IVb clearance) aiming for R0 margins while preserving adequate FLR.  
• If R0 resection is achievable, proceed with liver surgery (single‑stage if FLR adequate, otherwise staged).  
• Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy to complete a total of 6–8 months of chemotherapy, with surveillance of CEA and imaging.

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
• Status of the primary colorectal tumor (resected vs pending).  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric data.  
• Detailed arterial and portal venous anatomy of the liver (arterial map, presence of portal thrombosis).  
• Results of liver MRI (lesion characterization, number of lesions, relationship to biliary structures).  
• Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered and the response achieved.  
• Timing of metastases (synchronous vs metachronous) and grade of differentiation of the primary tumor.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five liver metastases, including a large 8.5 cm lesion in segment IVb with bilateral portal contact, in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and elevated CEA (870 ng/mL). The central location, size, and bilateral portal involvement make a safe R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant technically uncertain at this stage. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only after tumor downsizing.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (870 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Mandatory induction systemic therapy
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology, particularly reduction of portal contact.

C. Expert vascular restaging
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the segment IVb lesion to both portal branches.
